newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. steps up efforts to clinch Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. steps up efforts to clinch Hebron deal.

text.p: The United States stepped up efforts on Sunday to clinch a deal between Israel and the PLO on implementing an Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.
U.S. President Bill Clinton telephoned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to urge them to wrap up three weeks of U.S.-mediated talks.
Netanyahu then called Arafat amid speculation both leaders could hold a late-night summit at the Erez Crossing between Israel and Gaza on Sunday or a morning meeting there on Monday.
Palestinian and Israeli officials gave no details of the Netanyahu-Arafat conversation except to say it dealt with Hebron.
In Washington, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had spoken to each leader for about 10 minutes.

Clinton, he said, had encouraged them "to do everything they can to address the remaining issues relating to Oslo (peace accords') implementation and specifically security related issues and the withdrawal from Hebron".

Asked why Clinton had taken the trouble to call both Arafat and Netanyahu, McCurry said: "They're down to some difficult issues ... the issues are difficult because the concerns on both sides are deeply held."

U.S. mediator Dennis Ross has been trying to seal an elusive deal on security arrangements in the town of 100,000 Palestinians and 400 Jewish settlers. Palestinians said the sides are still far apart.

The U.S. envoy, who held talks with Netanyahu in northern Israel on Sunday, met Arafat for two hours in Gaza later in the day, part of last-minute efforts to finalise an agreement before the Palestinian leader's planned departure for Europe on Monday.
"We are continuing the efforts to see if we can find a way to overcome the differences," Ross told reporters after meeting Arafat. "We are working hard, trying to do so."
Earlier on Sunday, top Netanyahu aide David Bar-Illan said the two sides were on the verge of an agreement which could be concluded at a summit between Netanyahu and Arafat.
Asked if Netanyahu would meet Arafat on Sunday, Bar-Illan said: "It may happen."

PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat said there were still "deep differences", including over Israel's demand for the right to pursue Palestinian militants into parts of Hebron vacated by Israel and what weapons Palestinian police would carry.
Netanyahu met Hebron settler leaders in his Jerusalem office but failed to win their support for security arrangements he has yet to spell out publicly.

"I am very afraid that the country is about to make a fatal mistake," settler leader Noam Arnon told Israel Radio, referring to the security deal. "I think (Netanyahu) is falling into a trap from which he will not be able to escape."

Netanyahu's spokesman said chief Israeli negotiator Dan Shomron explained to the settlers "some of the security adjustments" under consideration and the prime minister promised them "he was doing his utmost to ensure (their) welfare and security".
Before travelling to Gaza, Ross said Arafat's four-day visit to Norway and Ireland would hamper mediation efforts.

"Clearly the pace of negotiations is affected when the leaders are not here. Also, my own presence is affected when the leaders aren't here because part of my mission is very clearly to go back and forth between the leaders," he said.

Israel's former Labour government agreed more than a year ago to redeploy troops away from Hebron but delayed the pullout after suicide bombings by Moslem militants killed 59 people in the Jewish state in February and March.
